title: Understanding Brain Tumours
condition_or_topic: Brain and spinal cord tumours in adults
clinical_background: Brain and spinal cord tumours are abnormal cell growths that may be benign or malignant. Either type can disrupt nervous system function and may require urgent treatment. Symptoms and treatment options depend on factors such as tumour location, type and grade. A diagnosis can also create emotional and practical challenges for affected people and their families.
objectives: Help adults with brain or spinal cord tumours, their families and friends understand how these tumours are diagnosed and treated.
Provide information about support services and help readers prepare questions for their treatment team.

population.description: The booklet is intended for adults with brain or spinal cord tumours and for their families and friends; it does not describe a study population.

clinical_implications: Both benign and malignant brain or spinal cord tumours can disrupt nervous system function, become life-threatening and require urgent treatment.
Tumour type, location, grade and genetic make-up, together with the person's health and symptoms, influence treatment choices and prognosis; the exact course of disease cannot be predicted.

A low-grade tumour or one that can be removed completely and safely may have a better prognosis. Some tumours, particularly gliomas, can continue growing, recur or transform into a higher-grade tumour.
Tumours and their treatments can cause lasting changes in cognition, speech, movement, behaviour and daily functioning, making rehabilitation and support relevant to care.
Immunotherapy is not currently a standard treatment for primary brain tumours, although it may be used for certain cancers that have spread to the brain.
practice_implications: Seek medical assessment for new, persistent or worsening symptoms. Discuss an individual diagnosis, prognosis and treatment options with the treating doctors.
Base treatment planning on tumour characteristics, symptoms, health and treatment aims. A multidisciplinary team may discuss the options.
Discuss treatment benefits, risks, side effects and alternatives before deciding; a second opinion or participation in a clinical trial may also be considered.
Report new or changing symptoms promptly during follow-up. After treatment, attend regular appointments to monitor health, long-term effects and tumour recurrence or spread.
Discuss treatment-related symptoms and rehabilitation needs with the care team. Do not stop or alter anticonvulsant medicines without a doctor's advice.

For a seizure, protect the person from injury without restraining them or putting anything in their mouth. Call Triple Zero (000) if it is their first seizure, they are injured, food or fluid is in their mouth, the seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes, or the response is uncertain.
Ask a doctor how the tumour or its treatment affects driving, and check with the doctor before driving again. Follow driving restrictions and applicable reporting requirements.

Tell the treating doctor about complementary therapies being used or considered. Cancer Council does not recommend alternative therapies in place of conventional cancer treatment because they may interfere with successful treatment and cause harm.
limitations: The booklet provides general information rather than individual medical advice and cannot identify the best treatment for a particular person.
Its principal focus is adults; childhood brain tumours may differ in location, treatment and outlook.
open_questions: The cause of most brain and spinal cord tumours remains unknown.
Research continues into possible long-term effects of mobile phone use, although research has not shown that it causes brain cancer.
future_directions: Researchers are investigating treatments directed at tumour genes such as BRAF, NTRK and IDH to support more personalised care.
Clinical trials are testing new immunotherapy approaches for primary brain tumours.

main_findings.description: An estimated 1900 malignant brain tumours are diagnosed each year in Australia.
main_findings.context: The booklet attributes this estimate to Australian cancer data; it is not a result of a study conducted for the booklet.

main_findings.description: About 110 children aged 0–14 are diagnosed with a malignant brain tumour each year in Australia.
main_findings.context: Australian estimate for children aged 0–14, attributed to Australian cancer data.

main_findings.description: There are more than 40 principal types of primary brain and spinal cord tumour.
main_findings.context: Descriptive classification information, not an outcome measured by the booklet.

main_findings.description: Glioblastoma accounts for more than half of gliomas.
main_findings.context: Descriptive information about tumour types, not an outcome measured by the booklet.

main_findings.description: In a personal account, Ali reported surgery for a grade 2 oligodendroglioma without additional treatment at that time. The tumour returned 9 years later. After a second operation, Ali received 6 weeks of radiation therapy followed by 6 months of oral chemotherapy, and described stomach inflammation, weight and strength loss, and impaired clarity of thought, with gradual improvement over time.
main_findings.context: Personal account in the booklet; no treatment-response measure is reported.

notable_adverse_events: Brain or spinal cord surgery: possible short-term or longer-term changes in speech, movement, behaviour and thinking.

Brain or spinal cord surgery: wound infection; the booklet describes the risk as small and notes that a small number of people may need another operation to clean the wound and possibly remove the bone flap.
Brain or spinal cord surgery: bleeding, described as rare but serious.
Brain surgery: swelling that raises intracranial pressure.
After surgery: headache or nausea.
After surgery: confusion, dizziness, speech difficulties, weakness in parts of the body and seizures may persist; these effects often improve with time.
After some operations: facial or eye swelling or bruising, which should ease in about a week.
Spinal cord surgery: possible nerve or spinal cord injury.
Radiation therapy: nausea that may begin several hours after treatment and headaches during the treatment course.
Radiation therapy: fatigue that worsens toward the end of treatment and may continue to build afterward, but usually improves over a month or so.
Radiation therapy: dry, itchy, red, sore or flaky skin in the treated area; it is usually mild, begins near the end of treatment and lasts 1–2 weeks.
Radiation therapy to the head: hair loss in the treated area, usually temporary but sometimes permanent; regrown hair may differ in texture or colour.
Radiation therapy: reduced hearing associated with fluid in the middle ear, usually temporary but potentially permanent.
Radiation therapy for a spinal cord tumour: temporary throat soreness or dryness and swallowing difficulty if the neck is treated, or temporary diarrhoea if the lower spine is treated.
Radiation therapy to the brain: in a small number of adults, memory problems, confusion or headaches may appear months or years after treatment.
High-dose radiation to the pituitary gland: reduced production of some hormones, potentially affecting body temperature, growth, sleep, weight and appetite.

Temozolomide: side effects are described as mostly mild and may include nausea or vomiting; tiredness, fatigue or low energy; increased infection risk; mouth sores or ulcers; diarrhoea or constipation; reduced appetite; and skin rash.

Temozolomide: possible liver damage, anaemia-associated breathlessness, thrombocytopenia-associated abnormal bleeding, reduced bone marrow blood-cell production and ovarian or testicular damage that may cause infertility.
Chemotherapy for brain and spinal cord tumours: hair may thin or become patchy in some cases, while complete hair loss is described as rare.
Steroids used short term: possible increased appetite, weight gain, sleep difficulty, restlessness, mood swings and anxiety; serious changes in thinking or behaviour are described as rare.
Steroids used short term in people with diabetes: blood sugar may rapidly become high or unstable.

Steroids taken for several months: possible fluid retention in the feet, hands or face; high blood pressure; weight gain; unstable blood sugar; diabetes; muscle weakness; reduced bone density; and greater susceptibility to infection.
Anticonvulsant medicines: possible tiredness, gum problems, tremors, nausea, vomiting, weight changes, depression, irritability and aggression; a rash may occur with an allergic reaction.
Contrast given before a CT scan: possible transient feeling of heat, bitter taste and sensation of needing to urinate, usually lasting only a couple of minutes.

diseases_and_conditions.context: Usually grows slowly, but can impair brain function and require urgent treatment.

diseases_and_conditions.context: May grow, spread within the nervous system or recur after treatment.

diseases_and_conditions.name: primary brain cancer
diseases_and_conditions.context: Begins in the brain and usually does not spread beyond the brain and spinal cord.

diseases_and_conditions.name: secondary cancer
diseases_and_conditions.context: Cancer originating elsewhere in the body that has spread to the brain.

diseases_and_conditions.name: metastasis
diseases_and_conditions.context: Describes cancer that has spread to the brain from another site.

diseases_and_conditions.name: melanoma
diseases_and_conditions.context: Listed among cancers most likely to spread to the brain.

diseases_and_conditions.name: lung cancer
diseases_and_conditions.context: Listed among cancers most likely to spread to the brain.

diseases_and_conditions.name: breast cancer
diseases_and_conditions.context: Listed among cancers most likely to spread to the brain.

diseases_and_conditions.name: kidney cancer
diseases_and_conditions.context: Listed among cancers most likely to spread to the brain.

diseases_and_conditions.name: bowel cancer
diseases_and_conditions.context: Listed among cancers most likely to spread to the brain.

diseases_and_conditions.name: glioma
diseases_and_conditions.context: The most common type of malignant brain tumour; it begins in glial cells.

diseases_and_conditions.name: astrocytoma
diseases_and_conditions.context: A tumour arising from astrocytes that may be benign or malignant.

diseases_and_conditions.name: glioblastoma
diseases_and_conditions.context: A malignant astrocytoma discussed in relation to surgery and chemoradiation.

diseases_and_conditions.name: oligodendroglioma
diseases_and_conditions.context: A malignant tumour arising from oligodendrocytes that may grow slowly or rapidly.

diseases_and_conditions.name: ependymoma
diseases_and_conditions.context: A tumour arising from ependymal cells that may be benign or malignant.

diseases_and_conditions.name: meningioma
diseases_and_conditions.context: A usually benign, slow-growing tumour arising in the meninges.

diseases_and_conditions.name: medulloblastoma
diseases_and_conditions.context: A malignant cerebellar tumour more common in children than adults.

diseases_and_conditions.name: pituitary tumour
diseases_and_conditions.context: A usually benign tumour arising in the pituitary gland.

diseases_and_conditions.name: schwannoma
diseases_and_conditions.context: A usually benign tumour arising from Schwann cells.

diseases_and_conditions.name: vestibular schwannoma
diseases_and_conditions.context: A usually benign nerve tumour that can affect hearing and balance.

diseases_and_conditions.name: acoustic neuroma
diseases_and_conditions.context: An alternative name given for vestibular schwannoma.

diseases_and_conditions.name: neuroendocrine tumours
diseases_and_conditions.context: The usual classification given for rare pineal gland tumours.

diseases_and_conditions.name: neurofibromatosis
diseases_and_conditions.context: An inherited condition that can lead to predominantly benign brain and spinal cord tumours.

diseases_and_conditions.name: childhood leukaemia
diseases_and_conditions.context: Prior head irradiation for this disease is discussed as a possible later risk factor for brain tumours.

diseases_and_conditions.name: overweight and obesity
diseases_and_conditions.context: High body weight is thought to be linked to a small number of meningiomas.

diseases_and_conditions.name: intracranial pressure
diseases_and_conditions.context: Pressure within the skull can rise because of a tumour, swelling or obstructed cerebrospinal fluid flow.

diseases_and_conditions.name: hydrocephalus
diseases_and_conditions.context: Accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid that may be caused by a tumour or occur after surgery.

diseases_and_conditions.name: seizure
diseases_and_conditions.context: A possible effect of a brain tumour or its treatment that may require anticonvulsants.

diseases_and_conditions.name: tonic-clonic seizure
diseases_and_conditions.context: Identified as the most common generalised seizure type.

diseases_and_conditions.name: aphasia
diseases_and_conditions.context: Impaired speech that may be addressed through speech therapy.

diseases_and_conditions.name: dysphagia
diseases_and_conditions.context: Difficulty swallowing that may be addressed by a speech pathologist.

diseases_and_conditions.name: anaemia
diseases_and_conditions.context: Low red blood cell levels are listed among possible effects of temozolomide.

diseases_and_conditions.name: thrombocytopenia
diseases_and_conditions.context: Low platelet levels are listed among possible effects of temozolomide.

diseases_and_conditions.name: infertile
diseases_and_conditions.context: The booklet describes possible loss of the ability to have children naturally after temozolomide.

diseases_and_conditions.name: osteoporosis
diseases_and_conditions.context: Loss of bone density is described as a possible effect of longer-term steroid use.

diseases_and_conditions.name: diabetes
diseases_and_conditions.context: Steroids can destabilise blood sugar in affected people, and longer-term use may cause this condition.

diseases_and_conditions.name: depression
diseases_and_conditions.context: Discussed as a possible difficulty after cancer treatment and as a potential anticonvulsant side effect.

diseases_and_conditions.name: claustrophobia
diseases_and_conditions.context: May make MRI scanning or use of a radiation immobilisation mask difficult.

drugs_and_therapies.name: surgery
drugs_and_therapies.context: May remove all or part of a tumour or obtain tissue for diagnosis.

drugs_and_therapies.name: total resection
drugs_and_therapies.context: Surgical removal of the entire tumour when this can be done safely.

drugs_and_therapies.name: partial resection
drugs_and_therapies.context: Removal of part of a tumour when complete removal is unsuitable.

drugs_and_therapies.name: debulking
drugs_and_therapies.context: Partial removal that may reduce pressure and improve some symptoms.

drugs_and_therapies.name: biopsy
drugs_and_therapies.context: Obtains tumour tissue for examination and molecular testing.

drugs_and_therapies.name: craniotomy
drugs_and_therapies.context: An operation through the skull to remove all or part of a brain tumour.

drugs_and_therapies.name: awake craniotomy
drugs_and_therapies.context: Allows speech or movement testing during surgery near areas controlling those functions.

drugs_and_therapies.name: brain mapping
drugs_and_therapies.context: Uses stimulation during surgery to locate important brain areas.

drugs_and_therapies.name: stereotactic surgery
drugs_and_therapies.context: Uses computer guidance to position instruments during brain surgery.

drugs_and_therapies.name: endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery
drugs_and_therapies.context: Removes pituitary or other tumours near the brain’s base through the nose.

drugs_and_therapies.name: laminectomy
drugs_and_therapies.context: Provides access for removal of a spinal cord tumour.

drugs_and_therapies.name: external ventricular drain
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Drains excess cerebrospinal fluid into a bag outside the body.
drugs_and_therapies.context: A temporary shunt used when cerebrospinal fluid accumulates.

drugs_and_therapies.name: permanent shunt
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Channels cerebrospinal fluid into the abdomen for absorption into the bloodstream.
drugs_and_therapies.context: An internal means of draining excess cerebrospinal fluid.

drugs_and_therapies.name: radiation therapy
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Uses controlled radiation to kill or damage cells in the treated area.
drugs_and_therapies.context: May be given after glioma surgery or alongside chemotherapy.

drugs_and_therapies.name: chemoradiation
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Combines radiation therapy with chemotherapy that makes cancer cells more sensitive to radiation.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Usually used for high-grade glioblastomas.

drugs_and_therapies.name: stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS)
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Delivers precisely targeted, high-dose radiation while limiting exposure of surrounding brain tissue.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Used for selected brain tumours, particularly cancers that have spread to the brain.

drugs_and_therapies.name: stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT)
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Delivers a longer course of precise radiation in multiple small daily doses.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Used particularly for benign brain tumours.

drugs_and_therapies.name: proton therapy
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Uses protons instead of x-ray beams for radiation treatment.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Used for some brain or spinal cord tumours and tumours near sensitive areas.

drugs_and_therapies.name: chemotherapy
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Uses drugs to kill cancer cells or slow their growth.
drugs_and_therapies.context: May be given after surgery or radiation therapy, or concurrently with radiation.

drugs_and_therapies.name: temozolomide
drugs_and_therapies.context: The most commonly prescribed chemotherapy drug described for grade 4 glioma brain tumours.

drugs_and_therapies.name: lomustine
drugs_and_therapies.context: Named as another chemotherapy drug that may be used.

drugs_and_therapies.name: PCV
drugs_and_therapies.context: A chemotherapy regimen named as another treatment option.

drugs_and_therapies.name: procarbazine
drugs_and_therapies.context: Named as a component of PCV.

drugs_and_therapies.name: vincristine
drugs_and_therapies.context: Named as a component of PCV.

drugs_and_therapies.name: targeted therapy
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Targets specific cancer-cell features to inhibit growth or spread.
drugs_and_therapies.context: Discussed as a drug-treatment approach and an option for some advanced or recurrent tumours.

drugs_and_therapies.name: bevacizumab
drugs_and_therapies.context: A targeted therapy that can be used for advanced brain cancer and is most helpful when the tumour causes brain swelling.

drugs_and_therapies.name: immunotherapy
drugs_and_therapies.context: Not currently a standard treatment for primary brain tumours; investigational approaches are described.

drugs_and_therapies.name: nivolumab
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Described among treatments intended to help the immune system recognise cancer cells.
drugs_and_therapies.context: An example of an immunotherapy drug being tested in clinical trials.

drugs_and_therapies.name: pembrolizumab
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Described among treatments intended to help the immune system recognise cancer cells.
drugs_and_therapies.context: An example of an immunotherapy drug being tested in clinical trials.

drugs_and_therapies.name: PEP-CMV
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Described as a vaccine against cancer cells.
drugs_and_therapies.context: An example of an immunotherapy approach being tested in clinical trials.

drugs_and_therapies.name: DCVax
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Described as a vaccine against cancer cells.
drugs_and_therapies.context: An example of an immunotherapy approach being tested in clinical trials.

drugs_and_therapies.name: PVSRIPO
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Described as a virus intended to infect cancer cells.
drugs_and_therapies.context: An example of an immunotherapy approach being tested in clinical trials.

drugs_and_therapies.name: G47Δ
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Described as a virus intended to infect cancer cells.
drugs_and_therapies.context: An example of an immunotherapy approach being tested in clinical trials.

drugs_and_therapies.name: CAR-T cell therapy
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Changes the patient’s own immune cells.
drugs_and_therapies.context: An example of an immunotherapy approach being tested in clinical trials.

drugs_and_therapies.name: steroids
drugs_and_therapies.mechanism: Reduce swelling in the brain associated with a tumour or its treatment.
drugs_and_therapies.context: May be given before, during or after surgery and radiation therapy.

drugs_and_therapies.name: dexamethasone
drugs_and_therapies.context: The steroid described as most commonly used for people with brain tumours.

drugs_and_therapies.name: anticonvulsants
drugs_and_therapies.context: Used to prevent or control seizures.

drugs_and_therapies.name: palliative treatment
drugs_and_therapies.context: Uses treatments to manage symptoms and support quality of life when a brain tumour is no longer curable.

drugs_and_therapies.name: palliative care
drugs_and_therapies.context: Addresses physical, emotional, cultural, spiritual and social needs.

drugs_and_therapies.name: rehabilitation
drugs_and_therapies.context: Helps people regain abilities or adapt to changes after a tumour or its treatment.

drugs_and_therapies.name: physiotherapy
drugs_and_therapies.context: Supports movement, strength and balance during recovery.

drugs_and_therapies.name: cognitive rehabilitation
drugs_and_therapies.context: Uses strategies to address changes in memory, language, concentration and planning.

drugs_and_therapies.name: speech therapy
drugs_and_therapies.context: May help with communication or swallowing difficulties.

drugs_and_therapies.name: occupational therapy
drugs_and_therapies.context: Offers strategies and aids for fatigue, daily activities and independence.

drugs_and_therapies.name: complementary therapies
drugs_and_therapies.context: Approaches used alongside conventional treatment that may help with stress, anxiety or mood.

drugs_and_therapies.name: alternative therapies
drugs_and_therapies.context: Cancer Council does not recommend their use instead of conventional cancer treatment.

scales_and_classifications.name: World Health Organization
scales_and_classifications.description: Identified as the source of the brain tumour grading system most commonly used in the booklet.

scales_and_classifications.name: grade 2
scales_and_classifications.description: Low-grade tumours that usually grow slowly but are more likely to recur and may become higher grade.

scales_and_classifications.name: grades 3 and 4
scales_and_classifications.description: High-grade, faster-growing malignant tumours that may spread within the brain and tend to recur.

scales_and_classifications.name: benign or malignant
scales_and_classifications.description: Classification discussed for brain tumours, whose implications can differ from those at other body sites.

scales_and_classifications.name: glioma and non-glioma tumours
scales_and_classifications.description: Groups primary tumours by their cell of origin and likely cellular behaviour.

scales_and_classifications.name: Generalised seizures
scales_and_classifications.description: Seizures involving the whole brain and typically the whole body.

scales_and_classifications.name: Focal seizures
scales_and_classifications.description: Seizures involving one brain area and affecting part of the body.

tables.title: Common types of primary brain tumours

rows: These tumours originate in brain glial (neuroglia) cells.
Arises from astrocytes; can be benign or malignant.
A malignant astrocytoma that can arise from a slow-growing astrocytoma; accounts for more than half of all gliomas and occurs in adults and children.
Arises from oligodendrocytes; occurs more often in younger adults and is malignant, with either slow or rapid growth.
Arises from ependymal cells; occurs more often in children than adults and can be benign or malignant.
These tumours arise from other cell types in the brain.
Arises in the meninges covering the brain and spinal cord; the most common primary brain tumour, usually benign and slow growing.
A malignant tumour arising in the cerebellum; more common in children and rare in adults.
Arises in the pituitary gland and is usually benign.
Arises from Schwann cells surrounding nerves in the brain and spinal cord; usually benign. Includes vestibular schwannomas, sometimes called acoustic neuromas.

tables.summary: The table groups primary tumours by cellular origin and describes their usual behaviour and age distribution.

tables.title: Common tumour symptoms by anatomical site

rows: Meninges: headache, vomiting, weakness of the arms or legs, and personality changes or confusion. Parietal lobe: difficulty reading or writing, reduced sensation in part of the body, difficulty distinguishing left from right, and difficulty locating nearby objects. Occipital lobe: partial or complete vision loss. Cerebellum: impaired coordination or balance, uncontrolled eye movements, stiff neck, dizziness, and staccato speech. Spinal cord: back or neck pain, tingling or numbness in the arms or legs, altered limb muscle tone, clumsiness or walking difficulty, bowel or bladder incontinence, and altered genital or anal sensation or erection problems.

tables.summary: The symptoms listed vary with the affected anatomical site.

rows: Low-grade tumours that usually grow slowly; they are more likely to recur after treatment and can become higher grade.
High-grade, faster-growing malignant tumours that can spread within the brain and tend to recur after treatment.

tables.summary: The table relates grade to growth, malignant behaviour and the potential for recurrence or progression.

tables.title: Key points about diagnosing brain tumours

rows: Possible manifestations include headache, nausea or vomiting, confusion or irritability, blurred or double vision, seizures, and weakness in parts of the body.

Physical examination assesses neurological function. Blood tests may assess general health and hormone levels, for example with pituitary tumours. MRI and CT provide brain images, sometimes with contrast. Other scans assess brain chemicals, blood flow or active tumour cells. Biopsy or resection provides tissue for microscopic examination and other testing.
Tests and scans help establish tumour type and grade. A grade from 1 to 4 describes growth behaviour and whether the tumour is benign or malignant.
Individual expectations about the disease should be discussed with the treating doctor.

tables.summary: The table condenses the booklet’s diagnostic information into symptoms, examination, imaging, tissue testing, grade and prognosis.

tables.title: Key points about treating brain tumours

rows: The principal treatments are surgery, radiation therapy and chemotherapy.
A tumour may be removed completely by total resection or partly by partial resection or debulking. Craniotomy is the most common brain operation; laminectomy is used to remove spinal cord tumours.
Targeted radiation, such as x-ray beams, damages or kills tumour cells. Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) delivers precisely directed, high-dose radiation for some tumours.
Drugs are used to kill cancer cells and may be given as swallowed capsules or tablets, or through an intravenous drip.
Drugs act on particular features of cancer cells to inhibit growth.
Steroids may reduce brain swelling, while anticonvulsants may control seizures.
Treatment can have short- or long-term effects; symptom management and the possible role of rehabilitation should be discussed with the care team.

tables.summary: The table outlines treatment modalities, their purposes, symptom-control medicines and the need to address adverse effects.

tables.title: Key points about living with a brain tumour

rows: The tumour or treatment may alter speech, personality, memory, thinking, movement, balance or coordination. Seizures may be managed with anticonvulsants. Fatigue can persist, and an occupational therapist can help people manage it.

Support depends on assessed needs, personal choices and service availability. Neuropsychology, speech pathology or occupational therapy may address cognitive difficulties; physiotherapy may improve movement, strength and balance; speech therapy may help communication or swallowing; and occupational therapy may support daily activities. Under a GP Management Plan or Team Care Arrangement, a Medicare rebate may be available for up to 5 allied-health visits each year.

A brain or spinal cord tumour or its treatment will probably limit driving and work, at least temporarily. Australian drivers must notify their licensing authority about an illness or injury that could impair safe driving.

main_conclusion: This guide presents diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation and support for adults with brain or spinal cord tumours as matters requiring individual discussion with the treating team. Both benign and malignant tumours can be serious, and care depends on tumour characteristics, symptoms and the person’s circumstances.
narrative_summary:
This Cancer Council Australia booklet is a clinical-guideline-based introduction for adults with brain or spinal cord tumours and their supporters, not a report of a new clinical study. It distinguishes primary tumours from cancers that spread to the brain and describes benign and malignant disease; either can threaten neurological function. It estimates that 1900 malignant brain tumours are diagnosed annually in Australia and explains that more than 40 main types of primary brain and spinal cord tumour exist. Symptoms depend on site, size and growth rate, and may include headache, seizures, visual change, weakness or cognitive difficulties.

Assessment includes neurological examination and usually MRI, with CT and other investigations used as appropriate. Biopsy or surgical tissue can establish tumour type and molecular features. Brain and spinal cord tumours are generally assigned a grade from 1 to 4. Treatment is individualised according to tumour features, health, symptoms and treatment goals. Options include resection, radiation therapy and chemotherapy; temozolomide is described as the most commonly prescribed chemotherapy for grade 4 glioma. Steroids may reduce brain swelling, and anticonvulsants may control seizures. The booklet also addresses treatment effects, rehabilitation, driving, follow-up and recurrence. It advises discussion of individual prognosis and treatment choices with clinicians and notes that immunotherapy is not currently a standard treatment for primary brain tumours.

document_sections.heading: About this booklet
document_sections.content: This guide addresses brain and spinal cord tumours in adults, including diagnosis, treatment and support. It provides general information rather than an individual treatment recommendation. Health professionals and people affected by cancer helped develop it using Australian and international clinical practice guidelines for brain tumours.

document_sections.heading: What is a tumour?
document_sections.content: A tumour is a mass formed by abnormal cell growth. Normally, new cells replace cells that die, support growth and repair injury; tumour cells instead continue multiplying without normal control. In solid cancers, these cells form a lump.

document_sections.heading: How are brain tumours classified?
document_sections.content: Brain tumours are commonly described as benign or malignant, but these labels have different implications in the brain than elsewhere in the body.

document_sections.heading: Benign tumours
document_sections.content: Many benign brain tumours grow slowly and are less likely to spread or recur if completely removed. They can nevertheless disrupt brain function, become life-threatening and require urgent treatment. Some become malignant or more aggressive over time.

document_sections.heading: Malignant tumours
document_sections.content: A malignant brain tumour may be termed brain cancer. Growth can be relatively slow or rapid. Enlargement, spread within the brain or to the spinal cord, and recurrence after treatment make these tumours life-threatening.

document_sections.heading: Primary cancer
document_sections.content: Primary brain cancer begins in the brain and may extend elsewhere in the nervous system. Unlike many other malignant tumours, it usually does not spread beyond the brain and spinal cord.

document_sections.heading: Secondary cancer
document_sections.content: Secondary brain cancer, or metastasis, begins elsewhere and reaches the brain through blood or lymphatic pathways. Melanoma and cancers of the lung, breast, kidney and bowel are the most likely to spread there. A metastasis retains the name of its original cancer; bowel cancer in the brain remains metastatic bowel cancer.

document_sections.heading: The brain and spinal cord
document_sections.content: The brain and spinal cord constitute the central nervous system (CNS), which controls mental and bodily functions. The brain interprets sensory information and directs muscles and organs; it governs movement, sensation, memory, thinking, personality, behaviour, balance and coordination. The spinal cord runs from the brain stem toward the lower back and connects the brain with the body through the peripheral nervous system. Vertebrae protect it within the spinal canal. The meninges cover the brain and spinal cord, while cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) surrounds and cushions them. The pituitary gland releases hormones into the blood that regulate growth, fertility, metabolism and development.

document_sections.heading: The parts of the brain and their functions
document_sections.content: The cerebrum is the largest brain region. Its 2 hemispheres each contain 4 principal lobes: frontal, parietal, occipital and temporal. The left hemisphere controls the right side of the body and, for most people, speech; the right controls the left side. The corpus callosum transfers information between hemispheres. The frontal lobe supports cognition, executive function, speech expression, emotion, personality and movement. The parietal lobe processes sensory input and spatial information; the occipital lobe processes vision; and the temporal lobe contributes to memory and understanding sounds and language. The cerebellum coordinates movement, posture and balance. The brain stem connects brain and spinal cord and regulates breathing, swallowing, heart rate, blood pressure and sleep. The pituitary gland makes hormones that regulate bodily functions.

document_sections.heading: What is a brain or spinal cord tumour?
document_sections.content: Abnormal cells form a mass in the brain or spinal cord. Both benign and malignant tumours can be serious and require urgent treatment. They are also called central nervous system or CNS tumours.

document_sections.heading: How common are they?
document_sections.content: In Australia, an estimated 1900 malignant brain tumours are diagnosed every year. They occur more often in men than women and at any age; about 110 children aged 0–14 receive this diagnosis annually. Benign brain and spinal cord tumours are more common than malignant ones. Brain tumour diagnosis becomes more likely with increasing age.

document_sections.heading: What types of tumours are there?
document_sections.content: There are more than 40 main types of primary brain and spinal cord tumour. They can arise anywhere in those organs and are grouped by cell of origin and expected behaviour based on genetic make-up. Glioma and non-glioma are major groupings; gliomas are the commonest malignant brain tumour type. The accompanying table describes common primary tumour types.

document_sections.heading: Common types of primary brain tumours
document_sections.content: The table groups primary tumours into those arising from glial cells and those beginning in other brain cells. It identifies astrocytoma, glioblastoma, oligodendroglioma and ependymoma as gliomas, and meningioma, medulloblastoma, pituitary tumour and schwannoma as non-gliomas.

document_sections.heading: What are the risk factors?
document_sections.content: The cause of most brain and spinal cord tumours is unknown, and brain cancer risk rises with age. Familial brain tumours are rare, but an inherited gene change can increase risk; neurofibromatosis, for example, may produce predominantly benign brain and spinal cord tumours. Having a parent, sibling or child with a primary brain tumour may sometimes indicate increased risk. Prior radiation therapy to the head, particularly for childhood leukaemia, may slightly raise the risk of a later brain tumour such as meningioma. Vinyl chloride, some pesticides, rubber manufacturing and petroleum refining have been linked with brain tumours. A small number of meningiomas are thought to be associated with overweight or obesity.

document_sections.heading: Mobile phones and microwave ovens
document_sections.content: Research has not shown that mobile phones cause brain cancer, although possible long-term effects remain under study. Concerned users can consider a hands-free headset, shorter calls or messaging. There is no evidence that a microwave oven in good condition emits electromagnetic radiation at levels harmful to people.

document_sections.heading: What are the symptoms?
document_sections.content: Symptoms vary with tumour site, size and growth rate and may emerge over days or weeks or develop over months or years. Because many overlap with other conditions, new, persistent or worsening symptoms warrant medical review. A tumour may raise intracranial pressure by occupying space, causing brain swelling or obstructing CSF flow. Possible effects include headache, often worse on waking; nausea or vomiting, often worse in the morning or after a change of position; confusion or irritability; blurred or double vision; seizures involving limbs or the whole body; weakness; impaired coordination; drowsiness or unconsciousness; and difficulty speaking or finding words.

document_sections.heading: Common tumour symptoms
document_sections.content: Tumour location affects the symptom pattern. Frontal lobe tumours may impair planning, organisation, social skills, behaviour, personality, mood, walking, smell, sight or speech and may cause facial or one-sided weakness. Temporal lobe tumours may impair recall, learning, comprehension or sound recognition and cause seizures with unusual sensations, smells or deja vu. Pituitary gland tumours may cause headache, peripheral or other visual loss, nausea, vomiting, erection difficulties, reduced sexual interest and thyroid or other hormonal changes. Brain stem tumours may cause poor coordination, swallowing or speech difficulties, double vision, facial weakness or numbness, limb weakness, fatigue and altered sleep–wake patterns. Meningeal tumours may cause headache, vomiting, limb weakness, personality change or confusion. Parietal lobe tumours may impair reading, writing, sensation, left–right discrimination or locating objects. Occipital lobe tumours may cause partial or complete visual loss. Cerebellar tumours may cause impaired balance or coordination, uncontrolled eye movement, neck stiffness, dizziness or staccato speech. Spinal cord tumours may cause back or neck pain, limb tingling or numbness, altered muscle tone, clumsiness, gait problems, bowel or bladder incontinence, altered genital or anal sensation, or erection problems.

document_sections.heading: Nerve and other tumours
document_sections.content: The effects of a cranial nerve tumour depend on the nerve involved. The most common nerve tumours, vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas), are usually benign and may produce hearing loss, dizziness and balance problems. Pineal gland tumours are very rare and are generally classified as neuroendocrine tumours.

document_sections.heading: Which health professionals will I see?
document_sections.content: A general practitioner (GP) or another doctor arranges initial assessment. If testing does not exclude a tumour, referral is usually to a specialist such as a neurosurgeon or neurologist for examination and further tests. Following diagnosis, treatment choices are often considered at a multidisciplinary team (MDT) meeting. Different professionals may provide care during and after treatment; the tables outline their roles.

document_sections.heading: Brain tumours in children
document_sections.content: Children’s brain tumours often arise in different regions from adult tumours and may have different treatment and outlook. Children are more likely to develop gliomas and medulloblastomas, including tumours in lower or posterior brain regions involved in sleep–wake function, movement and coordination.

document_sections.heading: Prognosis
document_sections.content: In general, children with malignant tumours have a better outlook than adults, and treatment improves signs of cancer in many children. Because the nervous system is still developing, tumour- or treatment-related physical, behavioural and learning difficulties may arise, sometimes only after several years.

document_sections.heading: Health professionals to see
document_sections.content: Paediatric oncologists specialise in treating children with brain and spinal cord tumours. After 16 years of age, some teenagers receive care in an adult ward or from an adolescent and young adult multidisciplinary team. Depending on the hospital, support may include music, play, art or child life therapists, alongside occupational therapists, physiotherapists and social workers.

document_sections.heading: Treatment
document_sections.content: For a child, treatment choices, expected effects and concerns should be discussed with the medical team.

document_sections.heading: Support
document_sections.content: A hospital social worker can offer emotional and practical help and identify services. Cancer Hub can connect affected families, young adults and children with organisations including Canteen, Camp Quality and Redkite.

document_sections.heading: Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Assessment begins with symptoms, medical history and physical examination. Suspected brain or spinal cord tumours prompt referral for tests to establish the diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: Physical examination
document_sections.content: A neurological examination assesses functions such as speech, hearing, vision and movement. It may include reflexes, limb strength, walking and coordination, responses to light touch or pinpricks, and arithmetic or memory tasks. The doctor may assess eye and pupil movements and inspect the eyes with an ophthalmoscope. Optic nerve swelling can be an early indication of increased pressure inside the skull.

document_sections.heading: Blood tests
document_sections.content: Blood testing usually assesses general health, but cannot detect or monitor most brain and spinal cord tumours. Blood or specialised urine testing may detect abnormal hormone levels when, for example, the pituitary gland is affected.

document_sections.heading: MRI scan
document_sections.content: MRI is usually recommended to investigate brain tumours and plan treatment. It uses a magnet and computer to produce detailed images; injected contrast may highlight abnormalities. Patients should disclose a pacemaker or metallic implant because the magnet can interfere with some pacemakers, although newer devices are often compatible. The enclosed, noisy scanner may cause anxiety or claustrophobia despite the painless examination; medication, support, ear protection and a distress button may help. An MRI takes 30–45 minutes and generally provides more detail than CT.

document_sections.heading: CT scan
document_sections.content: CT may be performed instead of MRI when MRI is not possible. It combines x-rays and computing to image internal structures. Intravenous contrast can improve clarity but may briefly cause warmth, a bitter taste or a sensation of needing to urinate. Preparation may take about 30 minutes; the painless scan itself takes about 10 minutes. Before imaging, patients should report allergies, previous contrast reactions, diabetes, kidney disease, pregnancy or breastfeeding.

document_sections.heading: Further tests
document_sections.content: Additional investigations may characterise a tumour and support treatment planning. MRS examines brain chemicals and is used more often to assess possible regrowth than alongside an initial MRI. MR tractography depicts brain pathways and may assist glioma treatment planning. MR perfusion assesses regional blood flow and can characterise tumours or be used after treatment. SPET or SPECT uses an injected radioactive fluid to depict cerebral blood flow; higher-flow areas appear brighter. PET uses an injected radioactive solution that cancer cells take up faster than normal cells, making them appear brighter. Lumbar puncture collects CSF for examination for cancer cells. Biopsy obtains tissue through an opening in the skull, through the nose or during tumour-removal surgery; a pathologist examines it to identify cancer and tumour type. Molecular testing examines biopsy tissue for tumour-cell gene changes, which may be acquired or inherited, to help characterise the tumour and guide treatment.

document_sections.heading: Grading tumours
document_sections.content: Grade reflects how tumour cells compare with normal cells and suggests growth rate. The system most commonly used for brain tumours is from the World Health Organization. Brain and spinal cord tumours usually receive a grade from 1 to 4: 1 is lowest and least aggressive, while 4 is highest and most aggressive. Primary brain and spinal cord tumours are generally not staged because most do not spread elsewhere in the body. The table describes the behaviour associated with each grade.

document_sections.heading: Prognosis
document_sections.content: An individual disease course cannot be predicted exactly. Prognosis may depend on tumour type, location, grade and genetics; age, general health and family history; damage to nearby healthy brain tissue; and treatment response. Either low-grade or high-grade disease can impair brain function and threaten life. Outlook may be better for a low-grade tumour or one that can be safely removed entirely. Some tumours, particularly gliomas, continue growing, recur or transform to a higher grade. Surgery, radiation therapy and/or chemotherapy may then be used to control growth as long as possible, relieve symptoms and preserve quality of life.

document_sections.heading: Key points about diagnosing brain tumours
document_sections.content: The summary table brings together possible tumour-related symptoms, neurological and blood examinations, imaging and tissue testing. These investigations help determine tumour type and grade; prognosis should be discussed with a doctor.

document_sections.heading: Making treatment decisions
document_sections.content: Patients should ask their specialist when treatment must begin, since a short wait may not affect its success, and seek an explanation of available options before deciding. Understanding the disease, possible benefits, adverse effects and costs can support an informed choice. It may be useful to ask whether the specialist participates in an MDT and whether treatment locally or at a specialist centre is most appropriate. Notes, a recording made with the doctor’s permission, or a companion may help retain information. Questions can also be raised with a specialist, cancer care coordinator or nurse. A second specialist opinion can clarify recommendations even after treatment has begun. Adults may accept or refuse offered treatment: some accept substantial adverse effects for a small, short-lived benefit, whereas others prioritise quality of life.

document_sections.heading: Should I join a clinical trial?
document_sections.content: Clinical trials evaluate new or modified treatments and diagnostic approaches against current methods. In a randomised treatment trial, assignment to the best existing treatment or a modified new treatment is by chance. Trials have contributed to improved cancer treatment and outcomes. A patient considering participation may consult a specialist, clinical trials nurse or GP, obtain another opinion and withdraw at any time.

document_sections.heading: Treatment
document_sections.content: Treatment depends on tumour type, size, grade, site and genetics; age, medical history and general health; symptoms; and whether the aim is removal, slowing growth or relief through tumour shrinkage and reduced swelling. The exact type may remain uncertain until biopsy or surgery, so initial planning may use the surgeon’s interpretation of scans. Surgery alone may suffice for a benign tumour. Malignant disease may be managed with surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy or targeted therapy. Steroids and anticonvulsants may manage swelling-related symptoms or seizures. Immunotherapy or another new or modified treatment may be offered through a clinical trial.

document_sections.heading: Surgery
document_sections.content: Neurosurgery may remove a whole tumour (total resection), remove part (partial resection or debulking), or establish a diagnosis by biopsy. Complete removal is pursued when safe. Partial removal may be considered for extensive tumours or those close to major vessels or important nervous structures and can reduce brain pressure and improve some symptoms.

document_sections.heading: When surgery is not possible
document_sections.content: A tumour may be deemed inoperable or unresectable if removal near critical brain structures would risk blindness, speech loss, paralysis or other serious harm. Needle biopsy is often still feasible and may guide treatment. The doctor can discuss other treatments and symptom control.

document_sections.heading: What to expect before surgery
document_sections.content: MRI or CT may be repeated for operative planning. Functional MRI (fMRI) can identify regions used during speech or movement tasks so the surgeon can avoid them; brain mapping may also locate them during surgery. Patients should disclose blood-thinning and other medicines and supplements, since some may need to be paused because of anaesthetic interactions. Stopping smoking or vaping before surgery is important because either increases complication risk.

document_sections.heading: Types of surgery
document_sections.content: Craniotomy is the commonest operation for a brain tumour and can remove all or part under general anaesthetic; a skull bone flap is replaced and secured afterward. Before surgery for high-grade glioma, a solution may make tumour tissue glow under blue light to aid removal while sparing normal brain. Brain mapping uses an electrode to identify important areas during surgery or awake craniotomy. Awake craniotomy may be recommended near speech or movement regions: the patient is generally anaesthetised initially, then awakened and asked to speak or move during part of the operation. Local anaesthetic numbs surrounding tissues, and the brain itself does not feel pain. Endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery is the commonest approach for pituitary or other skull-base tumours, reaching the tumour through the nose under general anaesthetic. Laminectomy is the commonest operation for spinal cord tumours; access is gained through skin, muscle and a vertebra, usually under general anaesthetic. Surgery involving the spinal cord itself may also be required and carries a risk of nerve or spinal cord injury.

document_sections.heading: Computer-assisted surgery
document_sections.content: Stereotactic surgery uses planning scans to generate three-dimensional images that guide instruments during craniotomy. Compared with surgery without computer assistance, it is described as safer and more accurate and needs a smaller opening in the skull.

document_sections.heading: What to expect after surgery
document_sections.content: Patients are closely observed for the first 12–24 hours and spend the first day or two in intensive or high-dependency care. The table of postoperative topics covers neurological monitoring, clot prevention, spinal wound care, rehabilitation, hospital stay and wound changes.

document_sections.heading: Checks and observations
document_sections.content: Nurses repeatedly assess breathing, vital signs, pupils, limb strength and function, and consciousness to monitor neurological recovery.

document_sections.heading: Pressure stockings
document_sections.content: Leg compression stockings help prevent postoperative blood clots. New leg pain or swelling or sudden breathing difficulty should be reported to a doctor or nurse.

document_sections.heading: Spinal cord checks
document_sections.content: After spinal cord surgery, nurses monitor limb movement and sensation. Lying flat for 2–5 days may support wound healing, and a physiotherapist can teach safer movement in bed and when getting up.

document_sections.heading: Rehabilitation
document_sections.content: Short- or longer-term postoperative effects may require rehabilitation before discharge to restore mobility and daily functioning. Hospital admission may last only 2 or up to 10 days, depending on complications and side effects.

document_sections.heading: Bandages and bruising
document_sections.content: Dressings vary in size, and some or all head hair may be shaved. Facial or eye swelling and bruising after some operations usually subsides in about a week. Sutures may dissolve or require removal, as may staples. Hair does not regrow within the scar, although other hair often conceals it.

document_sections.heading: Headaches and nausea
document_sections.content: Postoperative headache and nausea may occur and can be treated with medicines.

document_sections.heading: Having a shunt
document_sections.content: Hydrocephalus is an uncommon accumulation of CSF that may result from a tumour or surgery. A temporary external ventricular drain directs excess fluid into a bag outside the body. A permanent internal shunt drains it into the abdomen, where it enters the bloodstream.

document_sections.heading: Side effects of surgery
document_sections.content: Wound infection is uncommon and can usually be treated with antibiotics, although a small number of patients need surgical cleaning and possibly removal of the bone flap, usually followed later by reconstruction. Bleeding is rare but serious; CT or MRI the next day checks for bleeding or swelling. Surgery may cause brain swelling and increased intracranial pressure, which the team monitors and tries to reduce with medication. Confusion, dizziness, speech difficulty, weakness and seizures may persist; patients may initially feel worse than before surgery, but these effects often improve.

document_sections.heading: Rehabilitation after surgery
document_sections.content: Some people gradually resume usual activities, while others experience lasting changes in speech, movement, behaviour or thinking. Rehabilitation can aid recovery or adaptation, beginning in hospital or a rehabilitation facility and continuing after discharge as outpatient care. Equipment may be supplied for home use, and driving may be temporarily restricted.

document_sections.heading: Radiation therapy
document_sections.content: Radiation therapy, or radiotherapy, applies a controlled dose of radiation, usually x-ray beams, to damage or kill tumour cells. For gliomas it is usually given after surgery, sometimes with chemotherapy (chemoradiation). CT or MRI and measurements define the treatment field to limit injury to adjacent healthy brain. Sessions are painless, although adverse effects are possible. For brain treatment a face mask maintains position; for spinal treatment small skin tattoos may mark the field. A usual schedule is once daily Monday to Friday for several weeks, often 3 or 6 weeks, but it varies with tumour type and size. A linear accelerator (LINAC) delivers sessions lasting about 10–15 minutes, with daily imaging used by most machines to verify positioning. High-grade glioblastomas usually receive radiation together with chemotherapy, whose drugs increase cancer-cell sensitivity to radiation.

document_sections.heading: Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS)
document_sections.content: SRS is radiation therapy rather than an operation. LINAC, Gamma Knife or CyberKnife machines deliver a precisely focused high dose while exposing surrounding healthy brain to little radiation. It is unsuitable for some brain tumours but may be offered instead of neurosurgery or when surgery cannot be done. It is used mainly for cancers metastatic to the brain; selected meningiomas, pituitary tumours, schwannomas and occasionally recurrent gliomas may also be treated. Often 2 or 3 doses suffice, although personalised courses may involve 1–5 doses. Sessions take 15–45 minutes, use a mask or frame, and are generally followed by discharge home.

document_sections.heading: Stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT)
document_sections.content: A stereotactic radiosurgery machine can instead deliver a longer series of small daily radiation doses, particularly for benign brain tumours; this approach is termed SRT.

document_sections.heading: Wearing an immobilisation mask
document_sections.content: A fitted mesh mask fixes the head in place for consistent targeting during brain radiation. It permits breathing and vision and is usually worn for about 10 or 20 minutes at a time. For claustrophobia or anxiety, the team may suggest relaxation, breathing strategies, psychological support or medication. Patients should tell the radiation therapist if the mask causes distress.

document_sections.heading: Proton therapy
document_sections.content: Proton therapy uses positively charged protons rather than x-ray beams and is used for some brain and spinal cord tumours or tumours near sensitive structures. A machine has been installed in South Australia, with treatment hoped to begin soon; funding currently permits overseas treatment for Australians in special cases.

document_sections.heading: Side effects of radiation therapy
document_sections.content: Effects generally occur in the treated area and are usually temporary, although some persist for months or years or become permanent. Possible effects include nausea several hours after treatment, headache during the course, fatigue that worsens toward the end and generally improves over a month or so, and mild local skin changes near course completion that last 1–2 weeks. Localised hair loss is usually temporary but may be permanent, and regrowth can differ in texture or colour. Reduced hearing from middle-ear fluid is usually temporary but may persist. Spinal treatment may temporarily cause throat soreness or dryness and swallowing problems if the neck is treated, or diarrhoea if the lower spine is treated. A small number of adults develop delayed memory problems, confusion or headache months or years after brain radiation. High-dose pituitary irradiation can reduce hormone production, affecting temperature, growth, sleep, weight and appetite; pituitary hormone levels are monitored during and after treatment.

document_sections.heading: Chemotherapy
document_sections.content: Chemotherapy uses drugs to kill cancer cells or slow their growth while aiming to minimise harm to healthy cells. It may follow surgery or radiation or accompany radiation as chemoradiation. Brain tumour treatment is usually swallowed as tablets or capsules, though intravenous treatment is possible. The blood–brain barrier restricts which chemotherapy drugs reach the brain. Temozolomide is the most commonly prescribed drug for grade 4 glioma brain tumours. It is taken at home in treatment cycles comprising specified dosing days followed by rest; treatment is likely to involve up to 6 cycles, though it may continue longer. Dose or drug may be changed to fit the patient. Other options named are lomustine and PCV (procarbazine, lomustine and vincristine).

document_sections.heading: Side effects of chemotherapy
document_sections.content: Adverse effects vary by drug and should be discussed with a doctor. With temozolomide they are mostly mild but may include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, infection risk, mouth ulcers, diarrhoea or constipation, reduced appetite, rash, liver injury, anaemia-related breathlessness, thrombocytopenia with increased bleeding risk, reduced marrow blood-cell production requiring regular blood tests, and ovarian or testicular damage that can cause infertility. Hair may thin or become patchy, but complete hair loss is rare with chemotherapy for brain and spinal cord tumours.

document_sections.heading: Ali’s story
document_sections.content: Ali recounts headache and collapse before diagnosis of grade 2 oligodendroglioma. Surgery followed within a week, with no further treatment then. The tumour returned 9 years later. After another operation, Ali underwent 6 weeks of radiation therapy followed by 6 months of oral chemotherapy. Reported difficulties included stomach inflammation, dietary restriction, loss of weight and strength, and impaired clarity of thought, followed by gradual improvement. This is an individual account rather than a general treatment outcome.

document_sections.heading: Targeted therapy
document_sections.content: Targeted therapy acts on particular cancer-cell characteristics to impede growth or spread. These drugs circulate through the body but are described as more focused than chemotherapy and often cause fewer adverse effects. Drugs matched to tumour molecular profiles are being developed; research in brain tumours includes targeting BRAF, NTRK and IDH to support personalised treatment.

document_sections.heading: Immunotherapy and brain tumours
document_sections.content: Immunotherapy is not currently standard for primary brain tumours, partly because of the brain’s immune system. Trials are testing approaches that improve immune recognition (nivolumab, pembrolizumab), cancer-cell vaccines (PEP-CMV, DCVax), viruses that infect cancer cells (PVSRIPO, G47Δ) and modified patient immune cells (CAR-T cell therapy). Immunotherapy may be used for certain cancers that have metastasised to the brain.

document_sections.heading: Steroids
document_sections.content: Brain tumours and their treatments may cause swelling. Steroids, or corticosteroids, may reduce it and can be given before, during or after surgery and radiation therapy. Dexamethasone is the steroid most commonly used for people with brain tumours; it is usually taken as a tablet but can be given intravenously.

document_sections.heading: Side effects of steroids
document_sections.content: Effects depend on dose and duration. Short-term use may increase appetite and weight, disturb sleep, cause restlessness, mood changes or anxiety, and rarely cause more serious thinking or behavioural changes. In people with diabetes, blood sugar may quickly become high or unstable. These effects can be managed, and taking steroids after food may reduce stomach irritation. Use for several months can cause fluid retention in hands, feet or face, high blood pressure, weight gain, unstable blood sugar, diabetes, muscle weakness, osteoporosis and greater infection susceptibility. A doctor may adjust the dose; most adverse effects resolve after treatment.

document_sections.heading: Anticonvulsants
document_sections.content: Anticonvulsants may be used to control seizures and can also affect mood or energy. Patients or families concerned about side effects should consult their care team; counselling or psychological or psychiatric support may help with mood and behavioural changes.

document_sections.heading: Palliative treatment
document_sections.content: When a brain tumour is no longer curable, palliative treatment aims to improve quality of life by controlling symptoms. It may slow cancer spread, relieve pain and address other symptoms using surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy or other medicines. It forms one part of palliative care, which addresses physical, emotional, cultural, spiritual and social needs and may be delivered at home, in hospital or in residential care.

document_sections.heading: Key points about treating brain tumours
document_sections.content: The summary table identifies surgery, radiation therapy and chemotherapy as main treatments and describes targeted therapy, steroids and anticonvulsants. It also notes that adverse effects may be short- or long-term and that symptom management and possible rehabilitation should be discussed with the care team.

document_sections.heading: Living with a brain or spinal cord tumour
document_sections.content: Tumours and treatment can affect speech, personality, memory, thinking, movement, balance and coordination. Fatigue is common, and an occupational therapist can suggest ways to manage it. Other effects depend on the affected brain region and treatment. Changes in behaviour or their effect on relationships and self-perception can be discussed with the care team or a counsellor.

document_sections.heading: Rehabilitation
document_sections.content: Rehabilitation helps restore abilities or adapt to injury- or disease-related changes. After brain or spinal cord tumour treatment, most people receive an assessment of rehabilitation needs. Available therapies depend on individual changes and can be delivered through a cancer centre, community service or rehabilitation hospital.

document_sections.heading: Types of rehabilitation
document_sections.content: The guide describes physiotherapy, cognitive rehabilitation, exercise, speech therapy, sight-related support and occupational therapy as approaches that may assist recovery.

document_sections.heading: Physiotherapy
document_sections.content: Physiotherapy may improve movement, strength and balance and teach techniques or walking-aid use to maintain independence despite weakness or fatigue. A neurophysiotherapist specialises in physical effects of CNS damage.

document_sections.heading: Cognitive rehabilitation
document_sections.content: Changes in memory, language, concentration, planning and problem-solving may be addressed by a neuropsychologist, speech pathologist or occupational therapist. Strategies can include memory methods, speech therapy, calendars, alerts and word puzzles.

document_sections.heading: Exercise
document_sections.content: A physiotherapist or exercise physiologist can advise on safe activity to improve circulation, mobility, heart and lung fitness and swelling, and help a person resume valued activities.

document_sections.heading: Speech therapy
document_sections.content: A speech pathologist may help restore speech affected by aphasia and address swallowing difficulty, termed dysphagia.

document_sections.heading: Sight
document_sections.content: A brain tumour may cause partial or complete visual loss according to the affected brain region. Vision Australia offers strategies for independent living.

document_sections.heading: Occupational therapy
document_sections.content: An occupational therapist may suggest aids and approaches for fatigue and physical or cognitive changes affecting personal care, meal preparation, work or driving, with the aim of preserving or improving independence.

document_sections.heading: Managing seizures
document_sections.content: Tumours or their treatment can disrupt normal brain electrical activity and cause seizures. Generalised seizures affect the whole brain and usually involve the whole body; the commonest type is tonic-clonic. Consciousness may be lost, muscles may stiffen, limbs may jerk, breathing may become shallow for up to 2 minutes, and tongue biting or loss of bladder or bowel control may occur. Focal seizures involve one brain area and may affect an arm or leg. Depending on location, symptoms may include twitching, altered sensation, speech difficulty, changed vision or hearing, unusual tastes or smells, deja vu, brief unconsciousness, mood change or memory loss around the event.

document_sections.heading: Ways to prevent seizures
document_sections.content: Anticonvulsant medicines can often prevent seizures. Overstimulation and marked tiredness can increase risk; the guide suggests 6–8 hours of sleep each night and notes that reducing alcohol may help.

document_sections.heading: How to help someone having a seizure
document_sections.content: Stay with the person, remain calm and consult their Seizure Management Plan if available. Do not restrain them or place anything in their mouth. Reduce injury hazards, help them to the floor when possible, loosen clothing and cushion the head and shoulders. Call Triple Zero (000) if it is a first seizure, injury occurs, food or fluid is in the mouth, the seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes, or the response is uncertain. Record seizure duration. After jerking ends, turn the person onto their side to protect the airway, especially after vomiting, with unconsciousness or with material in the mouth. Continue observing until recovery or ambulance arrival, explain what occurred and allow rest. If the person is in a vehicle or wheelchair, support their head and leave restraints in place until the seizure ends; then move and turn them onto their side if feasible and indicated.

document_sections.heading: Anticonvulsant medicines
document_sections.content: Different anticonvulsants may prevent seizures; blood tests may assess whether the dose is effective and how the liver is handling treatment. Possible adverse effects include fatigue, gum problems, tremor, nausea, vomiting, weight change, depression, irritability and aggression. Allergy may cause rash. Skin changes or other effects should be reported so a doctor can adjust the dose or medicine. Patients should not stop or alter treatment without medical advice. Some foods may need to be avoided, and herbal medicines can affect some anticonvulsants; interactions should be checked with a doctor or pharmacist.

document_sections.heading: Driving
document_sections.content: Brain tumours, seizures, surgery, anticonvulsants and some pain medicines may impair vision, concentration, planning, processing speed, reaction time, memory or coordination needed for safe driving. Patients diagnosed with any brain tumour should ask how disease or treatment affects driving. A doctor usually advises a temporary pause, including after surgery and sometimes radiation therapy. Exclusion periods apply after certain events or treatments; after seizures, and also after stopping anticonvulsants, a legally required seizure-free period precedes driving. Patients should consult their doctor before resuming. Australian law requires notification to the driver licensing authority of a lasting illness or injury likely to affect driving, and the authority may request medical information.

document_sections.heading: How to return to driving
document_sections.content: A driving assessment may include an off-road evaluation or electroencephalogram (EEG) to assess seizure risk. An occupational therapist driving assessor, neurologist or rehabilitation specialist may identify barriers to safe driving. An occupational therapist may teach compensatory techniques or suggest vehicle changes. Restrictions may limit driving to daylight, automatic vehicles or short trips. Driving must not resume against a doctor’s assessment of unsafety unless that decision changes. Ignoring restrictions can lead to licence suspension or cancellation, fines, criminal charges after a crash and loss of insurance validity.

document_sections.heading: Working
document_sections.content: Recovery and return to employment are difficult to predict and depend partly on job demands. Concentration or decision-making may be affected after treatment, making heavy machinery or substantial responsibility unsafe at first. Doctors and an occupational therapist can advise on returning. Adjusted hours or duties may help, although some people cannot resume their previous role. The National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) may fund supports for Australians aged under 65 with permanent and significant disability affecting daily activities. Under a Chronic Disease GP Management Plan or Team Care Arrangement, referral to rehabilitation may qualify for a Medicare rebate for up to 5 visits each year.

document_sections.heading: Key points about living with a brain tumour
document_sections.content: The summary table covers possible changes in cognition, speech, movement and personality, as well as seizures and fatigue. It outlines rehabilitation approaches and notes that brain or spinal cord tumours or their treatment are likely to limit driving and work for at least a period after treatment. Australian drivers must report conditions that may impair safe driving to the licensing authority.

document_sections.heading: Looking after yourself
document_sections.content: A dietitian can help tailor nutrition to treatment-related needs. Suitable physical activity may lessen fatigue, improve circulation and support mood, according to prior activity, current wellbeing and medical advice. Massage, relaxation and acupuncture used alongside conventional care may improve perceived control, stress, anxiety or mood; patients should tell their doctor about these therapies because some may be unsafe or lack evidence. Alternative therapies used instead of conventional cancer care are not recommended by Cancer Council: they are unlikely to have been scientifically tested, may interfere with successful cancer treatment and can cause harm. Financial advice and workplace discussion may assist with changed income or expenses. Cancer can strain relationships but may also change values or priorities positively. Sexual effects vary with treatment, adverse effects, confidence and relationships; intimacy need not depend on intercourse. Contraceptive precautions may be needed temporarily, and fertility effects may be temporary or permanent; people who wish to have children should discuss options before treatment.

document_sections.heading: Life after treatment
document_sections.content: Some people continue regular treatment. Others face physical and emotional adjustment after treatment ends, including mixed feelings, pressure to resume previous routines and concern about recurrence. Patients and families may need time to adapt at their own pace.

document_sections.heading: Dealing with feelings of sadness
document_sections.content: Persistent sadness, difficulty getting up or loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities may indicate depression, which is quite common after cancer. A GP can discuss counselling or medication, even for a short period.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up appointments
document_sections.content: Regular reviews after treatment monitor health, long-term effects and tumour recurrence or spread. These usually include examination and may include blood tests or MRI. Frequency depends on tumour and treatment. New or changing symptoms or health concerns between visits should be reported to the doctor immediately.

document_sections.heading: What if the tumour returns?
document_sections.content: A brain or spinal cord tumour may recur or continue growing despite treatment. Options depend on individual circumstances and prior care and may include surgery, radiation combined with drug treatment including chemotherapy, or another systemic therapy. Bevacizumab can be used for advanced brain cancer and is most helpful when the tumour causes brain swelling; benefits and risks should be discussed with the doctor. Other targeted drugs and immunotherapy may be accessible in clinical trials.

document_sections.heading: Caring for someone with cancer
document_sections.content: Caring for a person with a brain or spinal cord tumour can be rewarding but also stressful. Carers are encouraged to protect their own physical and emotional health and seek help. Home assistance, visiting nurses, peer groups, education programmes and counselling may address practical and emotional needs, although availability varies.

document_sections.heading: Seeking support
document_sections.content: Cancer can affect emotions, finances and daily life. Possible support includes treatment information, financial benefits, home services, equipment, groups and counselling. Services vary by location and may be free or carry a cost; hospital social workers, nurses and Cancer Council can help identify options.

document_sections.heading: Glossary
document_sections.content: The glossary defines the clinical terms used in the guide, including tumour types, CNS anatomy, diagnostic tests, tumour grading, symptoms, surgical and radiation procedures, systemic treatments, palliative care and rehabilitation. It identifies glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) as an earlier name for glioblastoma, distinguishes low-grade tumours as grade 1 or 2 from high-grade tumours as grade 3 or 4, and notes that even slow-growing low-grade disease may threaten life. It also describes pineal gland production of hormones including melatonin and identifies primary brain cancer as usually confined to the brain or spinal cord.
